subject: law
title: Unit 2.4 - Civil Liberty
intro: This source is a blank viewing worksheet, not a transcript or answer key. Use it to collect evidence about wartime democracy, the Gobitas children and constitutional liberty; the supplied document alone does not establish every requested answer.

lessons.title: Three kinds of questions need different evidence

source_refs.locator: A Nation of Liberties worksheet, two video sections

blocks.text: The first section asks what principles the Allies were defending, how World War II changed America and what tensions the interview describes. Some questions ask for historical evidence; others ask you to interpret a speaker’s metaphor about the Supreme Court moving in fits and starts.

source_refs.locator: A Nation of Liberties worksheet, two video sections

blocks.text: The second section asks why the Gobitas children refused a pledge and salute, which liberty and amendment they claimed, the lower-court outcome and the Supreme Court’s reasoning. Those prompts identify the issues to investigate; they do not supply the missing video evidence.

source_refs.locator: A Nation of Liberties worksheet, two video sections

blocks.text: The worksheet states that Justice Felix Frankfurter wrote an 8–1 Supreme Court opinion. It does not state the holding in the blank answer space. Do not mistake a question for its answer.

source_refs.locator: A Nation of Liberties worksheet, two video sections

lessons.summary: Separate historical evidence, interpretation and personal evaluation when answering the Supreme Court viewing questions.

lessons.title: Build an evidence-based case note

source_refs.locator: A Nation of Liberties worksheet, two video sections

blocks.text: Keep the factual question separate from your evaluation. If asked why a government might require a pledge, state that you are considering a possible justification; if asked what the Court decided, record evidence of the actual decision. A personal view cannot substitute for the latter.
